metadata.title: Should You Respond to an Infringement Letter Right Away?
metadata.purpose: Answer what comes first when an infringement or cease-and-desist letter lands: responding, or triaging it first. Lands the carry-out that tone tells you nothing about merit -- triage sorts by what's actually claimed so the one letter that matters doesn't wait behind a stack of form threats.

beats.narration_text: Someone gets an infringement letter and reaches to respond right away. Wrong instinct -- the first job isn't a reply, it's triage. Not a judgement on the letter, a sort against the machinery of one. Liam, in for Bear -- take them through it.

beats.narration_text: Every infringement letter is designed to read like a fire -- cease-and-desist language, a threat to sue, a deadline in bold. That design works: the reflex is to send each one straight to counsel. Here's what's actually happening. Most incoming claims are form letters -- one template mailed to hundreds of companies, no evidence attached, nothing specific to your product. They optimized for breadth and cheap intimidation. Route every one of those to an attorney, and the one letter that isn't a form waits in the same line as ninety-nine that are.

shot.new_visual_element: A stack of letters glowing with bold alarming language (CEASE, IMMEDIATELY); one plain-looking letter sliding in beneath the stack, unmarked and unlit

production_viz.label: Tone is not the same as merit
production_viz.mechanic: A stack of three letter cards, each with bold red words (CEASE / IMMEDIATELY / OR ELSE) fully lit, arranged fanned out. A fourth, plain card slides in from below the stack, dim and unlit, with no bold words, passing underneath without joining the fan. A caption fades in beneath: 'the one that's different waits in the same line.'

beats.narration_text: Triage runs four checks against every claim. Who is actually asserting it. What specific right they're claiming. What evidence is attached. What deadline they're demanding. Four fields -- pick any one that comes up empty and you already know the letter's shape. Watch the anchor: a letter saying your new packaging copies a competitor's, three exclamation points, no attachments, nothing filled in any of the four fields yet.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR -- four field chips lighting in turn (asserter / right claimed / evidence attached / deadline demanded), then a dim, unlabeled letter card set off to the side

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR -- four checks, then the unscored letter
production_viz.mechanic: Four chips fade in one at a time across the top, each labelled with a check (who's asserting / right claimed / evidence attached / deadline demanded), then fade out together. THE ANCHOR. A single card appears off to the side, dim and outlined only, reading 'packaging letter' with three exclamation marks and no fields filled in -- visibly unscored against the four-check shape just shown. THIS EXACT CARD RETURNS, FILLED IN, AT B03.

beats.narration_text: The packaging letter runs through the same four checks and every field fills in. Asserter -- a real competitor with a registered design. Right -- that design. Evidence -- a side-by-side photo. Deadline -- ten days out. That combination is what escalates it. Not the three exclamation points. Now the honest part: clearing every check doesn't prove the claim has merit. It means the shape is real enough that an attorney has to look. And in the other direction -- a bare form letter with nothing attached isn't zero risk forever. Sent again with evidence, it can turn into exactly this.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- the dim card lighting up with all four fields filled and sliding into the main list; then split into 'checked is not valid' and 'bare today is not ignorable forever'

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- checked, not cleared
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 DIM CARD RETURNS, identical placement, and fills in one field at a time (asserter / right claimed / evidence attached / deadline demanded) until fully lit, then slides into a row alongside other completed entries. It splits into two cards: left reads 'four checks: clear' with a struck-through 'VALID' beneath it labelled 'checked is not valid'; right reads 'form letter: no attachments' with a faint new card appearing at its edge labelled 'bare today is not ignorable forever'.

beats.narration_text: An infringement letter's tone tells you nothing about its merit. Triage sorts on what's actually claimed -- asserter, right, evidence, deadline -- so the one letter that matters doesn't wait behind a stack of form threats.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's a prompt to paste straight into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. I have an infringement or cease-and-desist letter I need to triage before I decide whether to send it to counsel. Read the letter I paste after this prompt and extract four fields exactly. Asserter -- who is actually claiming, and whether they appear to be a real party. Right claimed -- the specific IP right, with the registration number or identifier if present. Evidence attached -- the specific evidence, images, or documents that come with the claim, or 'none'. Deadline demanded -- the exact date, and how many days from today. Then grade the letter -- form threat, warrants attorney review, or urgent -- based only on which fields are empty. Do not opine on whether the claim has merit; that's the attorney's job. Go deeper: if the letter comes back as a form threat today, what would have to change in a follow-up letter to move it to urgent, and how would you keep a record of the original so you'd spot the escalation. Liam, in for Bear.
